name: NIST Already Has Standards
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Standard Already Shipped
lesson.summary: NIST finalized official post-quantum cryptography standards in August 2024 after an eight year public competition, a concrete, checkable deliverable that turns the promise in Post-Quantum Crypto Exists into a downloadable specification anyone can implement today.
lesson.body:
The United States National Institute of Standards and Technology, NIST, runs the process that decides which cryptographic algorithms become official standards for government and, in practice, much of the private sector worldwide, because so much software and hardware is built to comply with NIST recommendations. In 2016, NIST opened a public competition to identify and standardize post-quantum cryptographic algorithms, inviting cryptographers worldwide to submit candidate designs, then spending years subjecting those candidates to open, adversarial analysis, with researchers explicitly encouraged to try to break each other's proposals. This is the same rigorous process NIST has used historically to select other major cryptographic standards, and it directly continues the research lineage described in the previous chapter.

The process worked through multiple rounds of elimination over roughly six years, narrowing dozens of submissions to a small set of finalists as weaknesses were discovered and candidates were strengthened or dropped. In 2022, NIST announced its first selected algorithms, and in August 2024 published the finalized standards themselves: FIPS 203, a lattice based algorithm for general encryption and key exchange, FIPS 204, a lattice based algorithm for digital signatures, and FIPS 205, a hash based algorithm for digital signatures offering a structurally different mathematical foundation as backup. These are not drafts or research papers. They are finished, official, government published federal standards, with specifications publicly available, ready to implement today.

This is about as concrete and falsifiable an answer as cryptography ever produces to something that could have remained an unfalsifiable timeline: not a vague promise that a solution is coming eventually, but a dated, published, specific document anyone can download and check. It is also a clean rebuttal to the moving goalposts pattern, because the goal was stated clearly in advance, in 2016, select and publish quantum resistant standards, and that goal was met, on a multi year but predictable timeline, with a specific, checkable deliverable at the end.

None of this means the work is finished. Publishing a standard is the starting line for adoption, not the finish line. Software libraries, hardware devices, browsers, banking systems, and government infrastructure all need to implement these standards, test them for performance and compatibility, and gradually retire the older RSA and elliptic curve systems they depend on, a process that realistically takes years given how deeply embedded older cryptography is. Major browsers and cloud providers have already begun rolling out hybrid implementations combining classical and post-quantum algorithms during this transition, sensible given these newer algorithms have had less real world exposure than RSA has built up over decades.

The bigger picture from this chapter is that a finished, government standardized, publicly available answer changes the correct emotional response to quantum computing's encryption threat considerably. This is not a field anxiously waiting to figure out what to do. It is a field that figured out what to do years ago, published the result through a rigorous, transparent process, and is now in the comparatively mundane, large scale work of rolling it out. That gap between solution exists and solution is fully deployed everywhere is exactly the space where the threat discussed next, data being harvested today for decryption at some future date, still has room to matter.
